A former professional collaborator complained that the company did not respond to his requests to object, restrict processing and erase his work email account after the collaboration ended. The company had redirected the account's mail to another company mailbox for at least seven months and gave no reply to the formal rights request. The Garante found breaches of data minimisation and of the rules on erasure and replying to data subjects, and fined the company EUR 15,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The DPA imposed a €2,000 fine on a controller that failed to reply to an access request. A lawyer is allowed to file the request on behalf of the data subject insofar as the controller can authenticate the latter.
The DPA found that national law grants the data subject access to medical records of her deceased father if the information might have a significant impact on her health.

The Catalan DPA fined a controller €3000 for violating the principle of confidentiality when it sent emails to numerous family members of patients at an occupational health center without using the blind copy option.
The DPA imposed a € 200,000 fine on a controller that granted a third party a duplicate SIM card without the data subject’s consent and without verifying the third party’s identity.

The Belgian DPA found the controller to have breached Article 15 GDPR in conjunction with Article 12(3) and (4) GDPR for having replied to the complainant's access request after the one-month deadline.

The Icelandic DPA held that the University examining a student’s use of a learning website in a course supervision system violated the transparency requirement in Art. 5(1)(a) GDPR. The lack of information regarding peer assessment violated Art. 12-13 GDPR.

The DPA fined a videogame company €90,000 for its use of forum moderators without proper data minimisation or security measures limiting their access to personal data. The controller paid a reduced fine of €72,000 in accordance with national law.

A controller installed a CCTV hidden in wall clocks within the neonatal ward. A loss or theft of CCTV memory cards caused a data breach, affecting 190 individuals. For violations found, the DPA imposed on the controller a total fine of PLN 1,145,891 (approximately €262,500).

The Belgian DPA's Litigation Chamber fined the data broker Black Tiger Belgium (formerly Bisnode Belgium) a total of EUR 174,640 through three separate fines. The company processed personal data on a large scale, relying on legitimate interest, without proactively and individually informing the people concerned, and kept the data for 15 years. It also failed to answer the complainants' access requests fully and its record of processing activities was incomplete. Besides the fines, the Chamber ordered corrective measures, including a halt to the B2B Data Quality service until data subjects are notified, and a permanent ban on processing data of people for whom no contact details exist.

The text is not the decision itself but the CNIL's overview table of sanctions from its restricted committee. The entry dated 15/01/2024 concerns a lawyer handled under the simplified procedure. It lists failure to cooperate with the CNIL and failure to respect the right to erasure, with an administrative fine of EUR 5,000. No reasoning, articles or reference number are given in this table.

The Romanian DPA concluded an investigation into Alior Bank's Bucharest branch, carried out in cooperation with the Polish authority after a former client complained. The client had asked for deletion of his data and had his accounts closed, yet the bank kept sending unsolicited e-mails and SMS messages, and earlier sent commercial e-mails despite an objection. The bank's centralised system in Poland kept monitoring former clients and messaging them after contracts ended, which the authority found to be processing for an incompatible purpose. It fined the bank 84,491.7 lei (about EUR 17,000) and ordered regular monitoring of compliance with Articles 5 and 6 GDPR, including reporting any needed system reconfiguration to the Polish head office.

The Italian DPA learned from press reports that the Municipality of Trento, with a research foundation, was testing AI systems (Marvel, Protector, Precrisis) using public-space cameras, microphones and social media data. After an investigation it found unlawful processing: breaches of fairness and transparency, no legal basis (including for special category and criminal-offence data), missing information to data subjects, unlawful disclosure to third parties and a deficient impact assessment. It fined the municipality EUR 50,000, banned further processing of the data collected and ordered its deletion, and ordered publication of the decision. Charges on Article 28 and on police access to Twitter network data were dropped.

A patient complained that an aesthetic medicine centre run by David S.r.l. posted on its public Instagram profile a video of him during a non-surgical rhinoplasty procedure. The company relied on a signed consent form and said the patient was not identifiable and that no health data was shown. The Garante found the processing unlawful: no valid legal basis, health data was disseminated contrary to the Italian Code ban, and the information notice was deficient. It fined the company EUR 8,000, ordered it to rewrite its information notice within 90 days, and ordered publication of the decision.

A doctor left medical prescriptions for patients in an unattended metal box outside his practice, accessible to anyone, mostly not in sealed envelopes; 67 prescriptions were found during checks in Feb-April 2023. The doctor claimed patients had consented and that the practice was occasional, and said he had removed the box, but filed no defence after the proceedings were opened. The Garante found violations of Articles 5, 9 and 32 GDPR and Article 2-septies(8) of the Italian Code, and fined him EUR 20,000, with publication of the decision.

The Garante investigated the company running the PIGNA portal, which lets banks and notaries exchange mortgage documents, after the National Council of Notaries asked for clarification. It found that the company sent notaries summary reports on open files on its own initiative, outside the banks' instructions, so it was acting as a controller. It did so without a valid legal basis and without proper information to the notaries. It also wrongly relied on legitimate interest, not contract, for notaries' registration and credentials. The late privacy notice had already been fixed. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, fined the company EUR 5,000, ordered it to bring the reporting processing into line within six months, and ordered publication.
The DPA fined a controller €2,000 for illegally using geolocation data of their employee outside the latter’s working hours.
The DPA found a recruitment agency to have breached Article 12 GDPR and Article 17 GDPR for contacting the data subject even after a deletion was confirmed to the data subject.
The DPA reprimanded Klarna Bank for refusing to rectify an email address linked to the data subject’s payment card unless the latter accepted to create a new account

The DPA found that a controller who fails to reply to an access request within the one-month limit violates Article 15 GDPR. However, corrective measures may be unnecessary if the controller eventually replies.
The controller was not ordered to take any specific measures after they missed the deadline to respond to data subject’s access request at they followed the DPA’s order to take a decision.
The Spanish DPA decided that Law 25/2007 did not release the controller from its obligation to give access to geolocation data in the case of an access request.

The Belgian DPA found that a controller violated Article 5(1) GDPR for not timely deleting a former employee's mailbox. The DPA stated that the mailbox must be deactivated on the last work day and the auto-reply within one month or 3 months in some exceptions.
The DPA issued a €12,100 fine against a controller that failed to comply with the orders of the DPA and continued the processing of personal data after an erasure request.

The DPA ordered a retail company to stop using on-site security cameras to monitor employees. The company had based this practice on its legitimate interests without considering the fundamental rights of the employees.

This is a mid-year press release from the Hamburg data protection authority summarising fines of EUR 130,000 imposed up to July 2024 across 14 proceedings. For this record, a hotel was fined EUR 16,000 because it collected and stored identity card data without a legal basis. The other fines in the release (advertising company, support ticket systems, logistics firm, online retailer, police officers, private individuals) relate to other cases.

This is a mid-year press release by the Hamburg data protection authority summarising 14 fine proceedings up to July 2024, totalling EUR 130,000. It is not a single decision. The part matching Fino's entry is a EUR 11,500 fine on a company in the advertising industry for breaching deletion obligations, whose IT system also had technical security gaps. Other fines in the release concern a hotel, support-ticket systems, a logistics firm, an online retailer, police officers and private persons.

This is an interim press release from the Hamburg data protection authority summarising fines imposed up to July 2024, totalling EUR 130,000 across 14 administrative offence proceedings. It covers many different cases, not a single decision. The one matching Fino's record is a logistics company that paid EUR 32,000 for improperly disposing of delivery-driver lists. No articles, reasoning or calculation for that fine are given.

This is the Berlin data protection authority's 2024 annual report, not a single decision. Section A.II.1 describes one fine of EUR 60,000 against a provider of a practice management platform and patient portal for security gaps. Patients could view practice email credentials and the registration data of other patients, and a faulty end-to-end encryption allowed a downgrade attack affecting 198 institutions and 1,623,732 patients. The authority applied the EDPB fining guidelines. It counted health data at risk against the provider, and counted cooperation, immediate shutdown of the systems, a catalogue of measures and prompt notification of those affected in its favour.

This is the Hessian DPA's 53rd annual report, not a single decision. In its fines chapter it describes a settlement procedure against a large financial company. Complaints showed late replies to access requests, sensitive customer documents sent to wrong recipients and telemarketing calls without consent. The company admitted the violations and cooperated, so the DPA discontinued proceedings on two violations and applied a fine reduction. Fines totalling EUR 496,000 were imposed and the notice became final.

The text is the 53rd annual report of the Hessian data protection commissioner, not a single decision. It describes many fine cases from 2024. The case matching Fino's entry concerns an IT company that sent advertising e-mails to over 2,700 people in a one-off campaign, including the complainant, who was never a customer and had not signed up. The processing had no valid consent and could not rest on legitimate interests because the unsolicited e-mail advertising rules were not met. The commissioner fined the company EUR 10,000, taking into account that it was a first offence, little data was involved, there was negligence and cooperation.

The French DPA fined NS Cards France, an electronic money distributor, €105,000 for keeping personal data longer than necessary, having incomplete privacy policies, failing to sufficiently secure personal data, and failing to seek user consent regarding not strictly necessary cookies.

Following 27 complaints, the CNIL carried out online inspections in October 2020 and June 2021 of a company's web domain and its email service. It found that cookies were placed on users' devices in France, including by about fifteen advertising companies, without valid consent. The CNIL held that it was competent, since the one-stop-shop does not apply to cookie operations under the ePrivacy rules and the French company counted as an establishment. It fined the company EUR 10,000,000 for breaching Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act and ordered the decision published, with the company no longer named after two years.

The French DPA imposed a €75,000 fine to TAGADAMEDIA for collecting personal data through forms that were deceptive by design which did not allow the controller to obtain valid consent under Article 6(1)(a) GDPR.
The DPA found an educational institution to have breached the principles of lawfulness and purpose limitation in processing the personal data of its students for marketing purposes.

The DPA held that it is unlawful to use data that was collected for marketing purposes to assess the creditworthiness of data subjects as this further processing violates the principle of purpose limitation under Article 5(1)(b) GDPR.

The Polish data protection authority handled a complaint about the processing and disclosure of a person's data by a company. The company did not answer the authority's requests for explanations, nor the notice that fine proceedings had been opened, nor the request for its financial data. The authority opened its own proceedings and found a breach of the duty to cooperate (Art. 31) and of the duty to give access to information (Art. 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR). It treated the breach as intentional and imposed a fine of PLN 18,864, about EUR 4,000. The decision is marked as final.

The Icelandic DPA held that a law establishing that political parties' ombudsmen wear a badge indicating the party they represent during elections constituted lawful processing under Article 6(1)(c) GDPR and Article 9(2) GDPR.

The Icelandic DPA held that a controller acted in violation of Article 32 GDPR by failing to locate all personal data requested by a data subject in the context of an access request under Article 15(3) GDPR.

The Belgian DPA investigated the controller’s practices following a data breach involving almost 90,000 data subjects. No violation was found since the data breach was an isolated incident and the controller complied with Article 33 GDPR.

The Polish data protection authority opened proceedings of its own motion against the Minister of Health after data on a doctor's prescription (health data) was taken from the national electronic health platform and published on the social network X. It found unlawful processing of special category data, failure to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures (WhatsApp was also used to pass on data), and failure to give the doctor the full information required on the breach. It fined the Minister PLN 100,000, the maximum for public finance sector bodies, and ordered security measures and notification of the data subject.

The Hungarian DPA found three joint controllers to have breached Article 6(1)(a) GDPR, Article 9(1) GDPR, as well as Article 12 and 13 GDPR for having unlawfully contacted a data subject after the latter had signed up to support a political movement.

A Polish consulate sent court correspondence for the Kraków District Court in a divorce case. The postal operator delivered it damaged and incomplete, and the Minister of Foreign Affairs notified the UODO of the breach. The court did not report the breach to the UODO or inform the people concerned, arguing that the UODO has no supervisory power over its judicial activity. The UODO found breaches of Articles 33(1),(3) and 34(1),(2) GDPR and imposed a fine of PLN 10,000. It also ordered the court to notify the four affected people (the parties and their two children) within 3 days, and discontinued the remainder of the proceedings.

The Dutch DPA investigated International Card Services (ICS), a credit and debit card issuer, after consumer signals and complaints about its re-identification of customers online from 2019 (the ID&V process). It found that ICS did not carry out a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) before introducing this large-scale processing, which was likely to pose a high risk. ICS's internal risk process and its parent bank's earlier analysis were held not to be equivalent to a DPIA. The AP fined ICS EUR 150,000 for breaching Article 35(1) GDPR, using the base amount of the policy category II and treating the seriousness as low.
The DPA could not examine whether the data subject’s rights were violated by the controller due to the controller’s immunity under international law.

The Icelandic DPA held that the National Police Commissioner, as a controller, was authorised under Article 6(1)(e) GDPR to carry out background checks on personal data of an applicant for a position as emergency operator. However, the controller failed to duly inform the applicant about the extent and purposes of processing.
The Icelandic DPA ordered a controller to remove a post from a social media platform which constituted processing in violation of Article 6(1)(f) GDPR.

The Polish DPA had ordered a company, in two final decisions of November and December 2022, to erase the personal data of two individuals who had complained. The company never collected the decisions or reminders, and never showed that it had complied. The DPA opened its own proceedings and fined the company PLN 23,580 (about EUR 5,000) under Article 83(6) GDPR for not complying with the corrective orders. The company, which the DPA treated as small-scale but profitable, did not provide its financial data or cooperate.

The DPA warned the City Tourist Board that while publishing photos of public events on public squares is lawful, publishing a specific photo of the applicant's minor daughter lacked legal basis and purpose under Articles 5 and 6 GDPR.
The French DPA fined a municipality €5,000 for failing to designate a DPO and to cooperate with the DPA, therefore violating Article 31 GDPR and Article 37(1)(a) GDPR.

The DPA fined a controller €5,900 for notifying a personal data breach in a too general way and over a month after the event occurred. After asking for further clarification, the DPA also found a violation of the duty to cooperate, as the controller provided an incomprehensible explanation.
The Austrian DPA imposed a fine in the amount of €9,500 on a controller for failing to comply with an access request of a data subject and instead deleting their personal data.

The Dutch DPA found that Uber breached the GDPR transparency rules towards its drivers. The guidance notes were offered only in English, and the response to an access request was not in an easily accessible form. The access/portability form was hard to reach in the driver app. The privacy statement was not specific enough on retention periods and on transfers, and it did not mention the right to data portability. The case began with complaints that a French NGO filed with the CNIL on behalf of 172 drivers, and the CNIL passed them to the AP. The AP imposed a joint administrative fine of EUR 10,000,000 on Uber B.V. and Uber Technologies Inc.

The Estonian DPA held that, when responding requests for access to information, professional entities must carry out a thorough balancing exercise to assess whether the personal data they hold are of public interest or are covered by the inviolability of private life, justifying any restriction to the access to information.

The French DPA, by conducting on-site inspections in Amazon France Logistique warehouses, found violations of Article 6, 5(1)(c),12, 13 and 32 GDPR in the context of extensive workplace surveillance and issued a €32 million fine.

The Austrian DPA imposed a fine of €20,000 on a controller for unlawfully making use of cameras recording its employees at work and for failing to maintain a record of its processing activities under Article 30 GDPR.
The Austrian DPA imposed a fine in the amount of €10,000 on a controller for failing to cooperate with the DPA in the context of a complaints procedure, thereby violating Article 31 GDPR.

The Romanian DPA completed an investigation into Hora Credit IFN SA after a complaint that the company emailed the complainant documents containing another client's personal data and kept sending messages after being told of the error. It found inadequate security, failure to notify the breach to the authority within 72 hours, and no proof of a reply to the complainant's access request about the source of his data. Three fines totalling EUR 24,000 (RON 119,296.8) were imposed, together with corrective measures requiring better security, training, an internal breach policy, informing the affected client and answering the complainant.
The Italian DPA imposed on Sirio S.p.A. a €1,000 fine for unlawfully processing personal data of an employee, as a deposit card linked to the latter was created without the data subject's consent.

A health trust in north Milan notified a personal data breach: a nurse employed there obtained a printout of her husband's Covid test result from a colleague, without any delegation, and the husband later complained. The Garante found that, since March 2020, the trust had configured its health dossier so that all nurses and hospital doctors could access all patients' data across all wards, regardless of involvement in care. It found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and (f), 9, 25 and 32 GDPR. It ordered the trust to restrict dossier access to staff involved in care and to introduce anomaly alerts within 90 days, and fined it EUR 40,000, with publication of the decision.
The DPA fined a doctor €1,500 for unauthorized access to a data subject’s medical records and for failing to explain her legal basis.

The DPA fined UK Ministry of Defence €409,080 (GBP 350,000) for disclosure of 265 unique email addresses of individuals seeking relocation from Afghanistan following the Taliban's ascent to power in the summer of 2021.

The DPA held that the right to a copy of personal data does not include the recording of a phone call with an employee of the controller, if the data subject was provided with a transcript of said call.

The DPA held a violation of the Regulation and its Protection of Natural Persons Against Data Processing of a Personal Character and the Free Circulation of this Data Law of 2018, Law 125(I)/2018, by the Examinations Service of Directorate of Higher Education of the Ministry of Education, Sports and Youth in relation to Statistical Processing Methods of the scores of the candidates who took part in the 2019 Written Examinations for Registration and Ranking in the Appointment Tables.

The Finnish DPA ordered a healthcare provider to reliably identify persons in its electronic healthcare appointment booking system. In its decision, the DPA stated that requesting a name and personal identity code is not enough to verify a person's identity.
The Belgian DPA proposed a settlement to a controller asking them to modify their cookie banner in order to comply with Article 4(11), 6(1)(a) and 7 GDPR.
The DPA found that Radio Télévision Belge de la Communauté Française did not use misleading cookie banners on their website.

Limit Call, a call centre selling electricity contracts by telephone, bought contact lists from a list provider in Moldova and called about 32,000 people without checking consent, privacy notices or the opposition register. After an earlier complaint and a EUR 10,000 fine for not replying to the Garante, the authority inspected the company in May 2023. It found missing information notices, no proven consent, no register check, a dead email address for data subject requests and insufficient cooperation. The Garante banned the unlawful processing, ordered deletion of the data and corrective measures, and fined the company EUR 60,000.

The Hungarian DPA reprimanded a controller for breaching Article 6(1)(f) GDPR. Although the surveillance system installed by the controller was legitimate, it covered a too wide area and, thus, the processing at the time of the complaint was not proportionate.

The controller, a Slovenian Ministry, was found to have infringed Article 15 GDPR in conjunction with Articles 12 and 14 of the Slovenian Data Protection Act since, at the time of the data subject's complaint with the Slovenian DPA, it did not fully comply with the complainant’s access request.

The Belgian DPA issued a preliminary decision in which it ordered the controller to comply with a request of the complainant to delete data used for direct marketing communication, following the complainant's objection request pursuant to Article 21 GDPR.

Examining the publication by a hospital of patients' data on Instagram, the Danish DPA found a violation of Article 6(1)(a) and Article 9(2)(a) GDPR. The DPA stated that the processing could not be based on consent since, due to the power asymmetries between patients and the hospital, patients could not have given their consent freely.

After an on-site inspection of NAV on 6 September 2023, the Norwegian DPA found that NAV's governance system and the confidentiality protection in its case-handling IT systems were inadequate, identifying 12 violations. On 27 November 2023 it sent a notice of intended decision proposing orders to fix the failings and an administrative fine of NOK 20 million. The fine was driven by long-term broad access to special-category data about many people and by intent, including ignoring earlier orders. This is only a preliminary notice; NAV could comment, and the final decision and amount were to be set later.

The Belgian DPA proposed a settlement between the data subject and Mediafin, a Belgian media group, concerning the setting of cookies on the website of the Belgian newspaper De Tijd. Inter alia, Mediafin should ensure that the withdrawal of consent in the cookie banner should not take more clicks than granting consent.

The DPA fined a controller for several infringements in handling the data of minors and parents: no proper and documented legal basis, information was confusing, partly untrue and not properly given, data were retained after consent was withdrawn.

The Belgian data protection authority held that the constant surveillance of employees in a shop by CCTV was in violation of the principle of data minimisation (Article 5(1)(c) GDPR), as the surveillance was not necessary for maintaining security.

A customer of Alpha Bank, acting for his partnership that fell victim to online fraud, requested access to CCTV footage of his branch visit and to web banking log files. The bank supplied the logs late and could not provide the footage because it had been deleted after its 45-day retention period had expired, before the request was handled. The Authority found that the bank breached the access right and the response deadline (Arts 15(1),(3) and 12(3)), and breached the lawfulness principle by deleting the data after the request. It imposed a fine of EUR 10,000.

A customer, acting as legal representative of a partnership that fell victim to online fraud, asked Alpha Bank for access to bank-branch CCTV footage of his visit and to web-banking logs. The bank answered about 13 days after the one-month deadline, gave the logs, but said the CCTV footage had already been deleted under its 45-day retention policy. The Authority found that the bank breached the right of access (Art. 15(1),(3)) together with Art. 12(3), because it neither supplied the copy nor told the complainant about an extension. It also found that deleting the footage after the access request breached the lawfulness principle (Art. 5(1)(a)). It imposed a fine of EUR 10,000.
The Cypriot DPA imposed a fine in the amount of €45,000 on the Open University of Cyprus for failing to put in place appropriate security measures according to Article 32 GDPR.

The Danish DPA issued a negative opinion regarding the City of Copenhagen’s plan to develop AI tools to identify citizens in need of rehabilitation, as the national law relied upon for the purposes of Article 6(1)(e) GDPR and Article 6(3) GDPR was not specific enough in relation to the scope of the AI’s use.

Fifty employees of Autostrade per l'Italia complained that the company never answered their access requests about the data used to calculate their severance pay (TFR) and related information. The company argued that the data were at issue in pending labour court cases and relied on a restriction of rights, and that employees could see their payslips on an internal platform. The Garante found that the company gave no proper reply to the access requests, breaching Articles 12 and 15 GDPR. It ordered the company to satisfy the requests within 60 days and fined it EUR 100,000, and ordered publication of the decision.

A former employee of Amazon Italia Transport complained that his access request under Article 15 GDPR, sent by certified email in September 2021, went unanswered within the legal deadline. The company replied only on 4 February 2022, after the Garante opened its inquiry, almost six months late. It also did not ask the person to narrow the broad request nor inform him of any extension and the reasons. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12 and 15 and imposed a fine of EUR 40,000, with publication of the decision.

A mother complained that psychiatric expert reports about her deceased son, including health and criminal-investigation data, were visible online. The reports came from training material of a medical course organised by Cluster S.r.l., which uploaded them to its management system and emailed a link to 26 participants. The link was reachable on the web without any authentication. The Garante found the processing unlawful under Articles 5 and 32 GDPR and fined Cluster EUR 18,000, also ordering publication of the decision. It saw no need for corrective measures because the link had been removed. It treated the earlier emailing of the link as time-barred, but the security failure as continuing until the investigation.

The Italian DPA upheld a data subject's complaint against Editoriale Argo S.r.l.. The controller was found to have disclosed in a newspaper article excessive personal data of the data subject, contrary to the principle of data minimisation.

A data subject filed a complaint against R.T.I. S.p.a. based on Article 17 GDPR for not removing from a video explicit content featuring her and then-Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi during a 2013 public event.

The DPA fined a lawyer €500 for unlawfully processing a data subject's personal data by sending a letter regarding his divorce to the data subject’s company email address, accessible by all employees.
In the context of a procedure under Article 60 GDPR, the Irish DPC reprimanded Microsoft Operations Ireland Limited for violations of Article 12(4) GDPR and Article 17 GDPR.

Following an inspection, the Danish DPA assessed that Rigsrevisionen, an independent institution conducting auditing on government-funded agencies and enterprises, performed its auditing activities on the basis of Article Article 6(1)(e) GDPR and in compliance with the principle of data minimisation, under Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.

Romania's data protection authority finished an investigation into Rompetrol Downstream SRL in October 2023. The investigation was opened after the company sent several personal data breach notifications between July 2021 and February 2022. Employees had accessed customer data in the company's software without authorisation and unlawfully disclosed it so that loans could be obtained from non-bank financial companies in the customers' names. The authority found a breach of Article 32 GDPR and imposed a contravention fine of 546,073 lei, stated as equivalent to EUR 110,000.

The DPA fined a company (controller) €10,000 for unsolicited communication, in violation of national Greek law, Article 11 (1) Act 3471/2006 (Protection of personal data & privacy in electronic communications).

The Slovenian DPA held that a data subject was entitled to be informed of the purposes of a controller's processing log under Article 15(1)(a) GDPR. However, the DPA noted that whether the data subject is entitled to the entire processing log under an access request, must be decided on a case-by-case basis depending on the contents of the log and and applicable limitations (including derogations).

The Belgian DPA reprimanded a controller, an online booking platform, for failing to comply with Article 12(3) GDPR and because Article 6(1)(f) GDPR was not a valid legal basis to publish personal data of health professionals on the platform.

A complainant said that a leasing company's property advertisement photo showed his car with a legible licence plate, and that his access request did not result in the photo being provided. The Authority found that the company breached the data minimisation principle (Art. 5(1)(c)) and the right of access (Art. 15(1)). It imposed two fines of EUR 10,000 each, EUR 20,000 in total. In setting them it took into account that the photo was deleted promptly after the erasure request and that only the complainant was affected.

The French DPA found that two French Ministries had breached Article 5(1)(b) GDPR. The Ministries had used the email addresses of 2,346,303 public servants to share a video promoting the pension reform - against the original purposes of the data processing, limited to administrative communications to employees.

The Danish DPA reprimanded the Agency for Digital Government for having used JavaScript in connection with MitID, the Danish digital ID. Even though there were widely known concerns with the programming language, the Agency utilised it without conducting a prior risk assessment, breaching, among others, Article 32(1) GDPR.

The Danish DPA banned the Government's Driving Licence app from continuing the processing of personal data of 2.26 million citizens who had not actively joined the app. This processing was found to be in breach of the data minimisation principle under Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.
The Hellenic DPA fined a controller €60,000 for unauthorised disclosure of personal data to a data subject's wife.

A municipal employee (head of the technical service) complained that the Mayor's decision naming her, together with a criminal complaint against her and a preliminary inquiry, was published in full on the Diavgeia transparency portal. Her personal data also appeared in a Financial Committee invitation and decision, and her erasure request was refused. The Authority found unlawful publication of the Mayor's decision (Art. 5(1)(a), 6(1)(c)) and fined the municipality EUR 2,000. It reprimanded the municipality for a second Mayor's decision, found a data minimisation breach (Art. 5(1)(c)) for the Financial Committee decision and invitation (EUR 1,000), and found an Art. 17(1) erasure breach (EUR 2,000). It ordered deletion and re-publication of the documents and recommended that the legislator set criteria for what personal data is published online.
The Austrian DPA decided that sharing personal data despite an existing prohibition of disclosure without informing the data subject violates the right to secrecy.

After an enforcement request from residents, the Dutch DPA investigated how the municipality of Voorschoten processed household waste collection data (the 'dump history' linked to bin and token chips). It found the municipality kept this data longer than necessary, so it had no valid legal basis for it, and did not properly inform residents about the processing. The DPA imposed an administrative fine of EUR 30,000. It started from category III, moved to category II, lowered the base fine to the band minimum of EUR 120,000, and then reduced it further for proportionality because the infringements were minor. The municipality had already ended the violations by shortening retention to 14 days and informing residents again.

The Belgian DPA held that a data processing agreement cannot be applied retroactively, as this would allow for the circumvention of Article 28(3) GDPR. Moreover, the DPA clarified that both the controller and processor are responsible for concluding the data processing agreement.

The EDPB issued an urgent binding decision pursuant to Article 66(2) GDPR ordering a ban on Meta Platforms Ireland’s processing of personal data collected on Meta’s products for behavioural advertising purposes on the basis of Article 6(1)(b) GDPR and Article 6(1)(f) GDPR .

The Belgian DPA found that a college's communication of the reasons for dismissal of one of its former teachers to their colleagues and students was in violation of Article 6(1)(f) GDPR. Including the reason for dismissal was not necessary.

Trade unions reported that Lombardy Region had published online a regional government resolution and a share sale contract whose annexes listed personal data of about 730 employees of transport and motorway companies, including pay, litigation and in one case health data. The file was freely downloadable and indexed by search engines for a long period. The Garante found there was no legal basis for publishing the data and that the ban on disseminating health data was breached. It fined the Region EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website. No further corrective measures were ordered because the data had been removed.

The Italian DPA found the controller, a condominium manager, in violation of Articles 5(1)(a) and 6 GDPR for unlawfully installing a video surveillance system without a required assembly resolution. The DPA imposed a €1,000 fine and a processing ban.

The DPA fined a medical institute €7,000 for a failure to implement appropriate security measures leading to the publication of a data subject’s personal data (including health data) in response to a review she left on Google, in violation of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR.
The Italian DPA ordered a controller to bring her processing of medical data for research purposes in compliance with GDPR requirements.

A local councillor complained about two articles in a daily newspaper (21 and 23 December 2021) that, with her photo, wrongly said she had been swabbed for Covid and was in isolation/quarantine. The publisher ignored her deletion requests sent the same day and did not respond to the Garante's requests or attend the hearing. The Garante found breaches of the lawfulness, fairness, minimisation and accuracy principles, the journalism rules, and the failure to respond to the data subject (Art. 12). It banned further dissemination of her data, including in the online archive, and fined the publisher EUR 20,000.
Following a request for prior consultation under Article 36 GDPR, the Italian DPA authorised a Hospital to process the health data of deceased patients in two medical studies.

A man registered in the Public Opposition Register received an unsolicited promotional call from a small Italian photovoltaic company, A.C. Group, which had obtained the number from a US list supplier via WhatsApp. The Garante found that the company telemarketed without verified informed consent, did not check the Opposition Register, gave inadequate information in its call script and could not demonstrate accountability over its supply chain. It banned processing of data collected without valid consent, ordered deletion of such data and the adoption of verification and tracking procedures, and fined the company EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision.
The DPA fined a private tutoring centre €3,000 for failing to provide information on tax receipts and non-cooperation with the supervisory authority.

The Slovenian DPA found that a controller failed to display its video surveillance notice on its premises in a way that adequately notified data subjects of the video surveillance. As a result, the controller had failed to meet its informational obligations under domestic law.

The Slovenian DPA decided that while the controller did not comply with the access request when the complaint was filed, it later remedied the violation by providing the complainant information regarding his application process for a public tender.
The DPA reprimanded a controller for video surveillance of work premises, as the monitored area was too large for the processing to be based on a legitimate interest of the controller.
The Cypriot DPA reprimanded the operator of a website for failing to comply with an access request in a timely manner under Article 12(3) GDPR.

An insurance company mistakenly e-mailed a compensation confirmation containing one customer's personal data to an unauthorised third party. It recorded the incident internally, judged the risk low and did not notify the data protection authority. The authority learned of it from the third party and opened proceedings of its own motion. It found a breach of Article 33(1) GDPR (no notification within 72 hours) and imposed a fine of PLN 103,752, about EUR 22,000. It treated the long duration, intent, a previous infringement and poor cooperation as aggravating, and found no mitigating factors for the fine.

IMY examined six complaints from Poland, Italy and the UK by people who kept receiving H&M newsletters after objecting to direct marketing. In each case H&M failed to stop the processing without undue delay, in some cases for up to about 18 months, because customer service unsubscribed people only from the general newsletter and not the customer-club newsletter. IMY found breaches of Articles 6(1), 12(2), 12(3) and 21(3) GDPR. It treated the six cases as linked processing of low seriousness, took the company's task force and technical fixes as mitigating, and imposed a fine of SEK 350,000.
The DPA fined the Ministry of Migration and Asylum € 175,000 for several GDPR violations in its surveillance of migrants in asylum facilities, including the unlawful processing of biometric data.

The Belgian DPA dismissed a complaint regarding disclosure of data by the communications officer of a political party to unauthorized persons, because the data subject had not provided sufficient evidence that their rights were violated.

The Estonian DPA upheld a complaint filed by noyb and declared that the controller transferred personal data to the U.S. in lack of any legal basis under the GDPR. The controller was ordered to stop the processing.

The French DPA fined GROUPE CANAL+ €600,000 after receiving 31 complaints for the failure to comply with several GDPR Articles. The fine relates in particular to ‘cold’ calls, the exercise of rights by the data subjects, safety issues concerning the company's employees’ passwords and the company’s failure to notify the DPA when a serious personal data breach took place in 2020.

The Italian DPA fined a controller €70,000 for unsolicited telemarketing calls, including to individuals registered to the Italian Public Opt-out Registry. The DPA found a systematic lack of GDPR compliance including Articles 5, 6, 12, and 13 GDPR.

A healthcare worker complained that colleagues had repeatedly accessed her health dossier at the Lodi hospital trust in 2019-2020, during the Covid pandemic, to find out her swab results, organise shifts and assess quality of care. The Garante found that the access was for purposes other than treatment, by staff not involved in her care, without valid consent, and that the dossier had no alert or full logging systems. It declared the processing unlawful, fined the trust EUR 40,000 and ordered it to put in place anomaly alerts and full access logging within 90 days. The decision is also published in full.

The Italian DPA issued a warning to a private person for installing a camera on the external wall of her house, which was also covering a nearby playground. The processing operation was in breach of the lawfulness and data minimisation principles.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) issued a decision on the processing of personal data by CaixaBank S.A., the controller, holding that the design of a cookie banner respected its “Guidelines on the use of cookies” of 2020.

DEYA X violated GDPR's data minimization principle Article 5(1)(c) by sharing an employee's personal and health data with multiple recipients without proper justification. The HDPA ordered DEYA X to create internal policies to ensure GDPR compliance. A fine of 1,000 euros was also imposed.
The DPA held that the media reporting on a leaked file containing PCR test results of several thousand individuals, and the non-disclosure of the source are protected by the journalistic privilege.

The Croatian data protection authority fined the debt collector EOS Matrix d.o.o. EUR 5.47 million after an anonymous complaint with a USB stick holding 181,641 individuals' data. The inspection found inadequate technical security, which meant the company could not explain how the data left its system. It also found processing of non-debtors' data without a legal basis and recording of health details, including diagnoses, without a legal basis or a valid Article 9 exception. Privacy policies wrongly said health data would not be processed, and the wording about call recording ("may be recorded") was unclear. Calls were recorded between May 2018 and January 2019 without a legal basis.

In the context of an Article 60 GDPR procedure, the Cypriot DPA reprimanded a controller for unlawfully asking a data subject’s ID when addressing an access request and for failing to inform its users properly about a data breach.

The Belgian DPA reprimanded a Flemish municipality for violating Article 5(1)(f) GDPR, Article 5(1)(a) GDPR, Article 5(2) GDPR, Article 12 GDPR, Article 13 GDPR, Article 14 GDPR, Article 24(1) GDPR, and Article 25 GDPR, as a result of their insufficient technical and organisational measures, and insufficient privacy policy.

In the context of a procedure under Article 60 GDPR, the Irish DPC reprimanded AirBnb Ireland for infringing the data processing principles of data minimisation and storage limitation and for invalidly relying on Article 6(1)(f) GDPR as a ground for processing, when retaining a data subject's ID documents.
